name: HTML <geolocation> element
plain: A browser-drawn button that asks for location; the click itself is the request.
meaning: Same data as Geolocation, but the request starts from a trusted button the site cannot disguise, so prompts only appear when the person asked. Chrome can also re-ask after a block.

web.api: <geolocation autolocate accuracymode="precise|approximate" watch onlocation=...>; element.position, element.error

access.prompt_ui: Browser-drawn button with fixed text and icon; a click opens the normal location prompt, re-reads silently if already granted, and offers a recovery path if blocked.
access.persistence: Same stored geolocation permission as the script API
steps: location event fires; read element.position or element.error

chrome.note: Developer blog 2026-01-13, generic <permission> element was an origin trial in Chrome 126 to 143

data.update: one-shot, or continuous with the watch attribute

fields.name: autolocate
fields.precision: only reuses an existing grant, never prompts on load

fields.name: style contrast
fields.precision: browser refuses low-contrast or disguised styling

limits.headline: Can show a browser made button that asks for your location when you tap it
limits.user_action: You tap the Use my location button drawn by the browser
can: Ask for your location when you tap the button
Share your position again quietly if you already allowed it
Offer a way to turn location back on if you blocked it
cannot: Ask in the background or without your tap
Change the button's text or icon to trick you
limits.reach_label: Only after you tap, then while allowed
limits.differs: Only Chrome and Edge have it so far. Firefox and Safari use the normal location prompt.

story.what_it_is: A button the browser draws that asks for location, so your click is the request.

marketing.name: HTML geolocation element
marketing.pitch: Chrome describes a built in button for location so people can grant access with one clear click and sites avoid pop up fatigue.

story.for_you: You see a button such as 'Use my location' that looks like part of your browser. You press it and the browser asks once. Because you clicked it yourself, there is less chance of a pop up scam.
story.for_makers: Makers get more yes answers because people trust a clear browser button. It avoids ugly pop ups that people block by reflex, which helps maps, delivery and booking funnels.

use_cases.example: A store locator shows a 'Use my location' button that finds the nearest shop.
A food order page uses the button so an address is filled in with one click.
A hotel search page uses it to show stays nearby.
A location based web game shows a 'Start playing here' button that unlocks nearby quests.
A ride web page sets pickup using the button.
The trusted button makes it harder for a fake page to trick people into a hidden location request.

technical_bounds: Cannot be restyled to hide or disguise it (contrast, opacity, size, transform checks)
Not in Firefox or Safari: feature detect with 'HTMLGeolocationElement' in window

legit_uses: Higher grant rates from clear intent (Immobiliare.it reported +20% successful flows)
abuse: Pushing the element everywhere to harvest location

history.change: Sister element <usermedia> for camera and microphone announced as available
